newsitem.title: CHINA: China warns Denmark against UN human rights motion.
newsitem.headline: China warns Denmark against UN human rights motion.

text.p: China on Monday called for talks, not confrontation, on its human rights record and warned Denmark that ties would be severely damaged if it pressed ahead with a motion to condemn Beijing in the United Nations.

Trumpeting successes in raising the standard of living of tens of millions of Chinese, in curbing official abuse of power and torture to extract confessions, human rights officials defended China's use of the death penalty and said political prisoners were common criminals convicted by due legal process.

"China is a developing country and democracy has to be a gradual process," Liu Hainian, director of China's human rights centre and head of the Institute of Law at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, told reporters.
"It is impossible for China to move very quickly," he said, adding that it would be some time before China could implement direct or general elections.
China could not afford to repeat the chaos of the 1966-76 radical Cultural Revolution, he said.
However, the officials lashed out at those nations critical of Beijing's human rights record, accusing them of interference in China's internal affairs.

"No country is perfect and the development of human rights goes hand in hand with social and economic development," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told the briefing on China's work to protect human rights.
He attributed differences among China and other countries over human rights to differing views, adding that these differences could be narrowed through dialogue.
Shen urged Denmark to think again before introducing a resolution this week on China's human rights record at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva.
"If Denmark insists on doing this it will end up as the biggest loser," Shen said. "We still hope Denmark will think seriously about the consequences of such action.
"I can say relations will be severely damaged in the political or economic and trade areas," he added.
Denmark said at the weekend it had decided to press ahead with a resolution to censure China at the 53-member U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva.

Speaking in the Netherlands, Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen, said he believed the resolution would be introduced in Geneva on Thursday and that several countries would back it, including the United States, European Union (EU) member Britain and some other EU countries.

China has fought off previous such resolutions by rallying enough support for "no action" motions annually since 1990 and was expected to succeed again this year with France, Germany, Spain and Italy unlikely to back the motion.
Every year since Beijing's bloody crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in 1989, China has gathered enough support to block resolutions condemning its human rights record.

"I believe there are some countries that do not want a dialogue on human rights and at the bottom of their hearts what they have in mind is just to make use of the human rights issue to interfere in China's internal affairs," Shen said.
Such countries were driving a wedge between China and other nations, Shen said. He did not identify the countries.
The human rights officials at the briefing dismissed suggestions that veteran democracy activist Wei Jingsheng had been convicted for expressing his opinion and said he was a common criminal.
Wei was sentenced to 14 years in jail for subversion in November 1995. He was convicted and sentenced to 15 years on similar charges after advocating democracy in 1979.

The officials also said China had no plans to abolish the death penalty, describing the punishment as a necessary deterrent against a rising tide of crime. China executes thousands of people each year but the exact number is a state secret.
